sections.title: The Security Filter Chain
sections.content:
Spring Security is built entirely on top of the Java Servlet Filter mechanism. Every HTTP request that arrives at your application passes through an ordered chain of filters before it ever reaches your controller. This chain is represented by the SecurityFilterChain bean, which you configure in a @Configuration class.

The key bridge between the Servlet container and the Spring application context is the DelegatingFilterProxy. It is a standard Servlet Filter registered in the container (e.g., Tomcat), but it delegates all work to a Spring-managed bean named springSecurityFilterChain. This design lets Spring Security participate in the filter pipeline without requiring the container to know anything about Spring's dependency injection.

Inside DelegatingFilterProxy lives the FilterChainProxy, which holds one or more SecurityFilterChain instances. Each SecurityFilterChain can match a specific URL pattern, so you can have entirely different security rules for /api/** vs /admin/**. The filters within each chain are applied in a fixed order: channel enforcement first, then session integration, then authentication filters, then authorization filters.

The ordering of filters is critical — placing a custom JWT filter before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter ensures tokens are validated before Spring tries its own form-based login. Spring Security provides the @Order annotation and the addFilterBefore/addFilterAfter methods on HttpSecurity to control this precisely.

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization
sections.content:
Authentication answers the question: "Who are you?" It is the process of verifying that a user's claimed identity is genuine — typically by checking a username/password pair, a JWT token, or an OAuth2 token. Once authenticated, the system has established a Principal: a representation of the logged-in entity (usually a User object or username string).

Authorization answers the question: "What are you allowed to do?" It happens after authentication and checks whether the authenticated principal has the required permissions to access a resource or perform an action. For example, an authenticated user might not be authorized to access the /admin endpoint unless they have the ROLE_ADMIN authority.

Spring Security models this with the Authentication interface. An Authentication object holds the principal, the credentials (password, erased after login), and a collection of GrantedAuthority objects representing roles and permissions. This object is the central artifact passed between authentication and authorization components.

The SecurityContextHolder is where Spring Security stores the Authentication object for the current request. By default it uses a ThreadLocal strategy, meaning each request thread has its own SecurityContext. Any code in that thread — service layer, DAO layer — can call SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() to retrieve the current user without it being explicitly passed around.

sections.title: SecurityContextHolder
sections.content:
The SecurityContextHolder is the heart of Spring Security's runtime model. It stores the SecurityContext, which in turn holds the Authentication object for whoever is currently interacting with the application. The default storage strategy is MODE_THREADLOCAL, meaning the context is stored in a ThreadLocal variable — each thread independently holds its own context.

This is populated early in the request lifecycle by SecurityContextPersistenceFilter (or SecurityContextHolderFilter in modern Spring Security 6). For session-based apps it loads the context from the HttpSession at the start of each request and saves it back at the end. For stateless JWT apps, a custom filter populates the context on every request by validating the token.

After successful authentication (e.g., your JwtAuthenticationFilter validates a token), you manually set the context: SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(authToken). From that point forward, any authorization check in that request thread will see this authentication. At the end of the request, the filter chain clears the context to prevent thread pool contamination.

Be careful in async code: if you use @Async or CompletableFuture, the spawned thread does NOT inherit the SecurityContext by default. You must configure Spring's SecurityContextHolder strategy to MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL or use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor to propagate the context to child threads.

sections.title: Default Spring Security Behavior
sections.content:
Adding the spring-boot-starter-security dependency to your project immediately activates a set of default protections — no configuration required. Understanding these defaults helps you know what you're working with before you customize anything.

By default, Spring Security auto-generates a random password logged to the console and creates a single user named 'user'. It enables HTTP Basic authentication (a browser prompt), form-based login at /login, and logout at /logout. Every URL in your application requires authentication. CSRF protection is enabled for all state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH).

Session management is configured as IF_REQUIRED: Spring creates an HTTP session when needed to store the SecurityContext. X-Frame-Options is set to DENY to prevent clickjacking. Sensitive headers like X-Content-Type-Options are added automatically.

In practice you will always override these defaults. For a REST API you typically disable form login, disable CSRF (since you use stateless JWT), set session management to STATELESS, define your URL authorization rules, and add your JWT filter. The key insight is that @EnableWebSecurity by itself does not override defaults — you must provide a SecurityFilterChain bean to replace the auto-configured one.

sections.title: AuthenticationManager and AuthenticationProvider
sections.content:
When authentication is attempted (user submits a form, sends a JWT, provides Basic credentials), the request ultimately reaches an AuthenticationManager. The AuthenticationManager has a single method: authenticate(Authentication authentication). It takes an unauthenticated Authentication object and returns a fully populated, authenticated one — or throws an AuthenticationException if authentication fails.

The standard implementation is ProviderManager. Rather than doing authentication itself, ProviderManager holds a list of AuthenticationProvider objects and delegates to each one in order. Each provider declares which type of Authentication it supports via the supports() method. The first provider that supports the given authentication type gets to try — if it throws AuthenticationException, the next provider is tried. This chained delegation is what allows Spring Security to handle multiple authentication mechanisms simultaneously (e.g., JWT tokens AND username/password form login in the same app).

DaoAuthenticationProvider is the most commonly used built-in provider. It handles UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken by loading user details from a UserDetailsService and comparing the submitted password against the stored one using a PasswordEncoder. Configuring it is straightforward: inject your UserDetailsService and PasswordEncoder into it and register it with your AuthenticationManager.

You can write custom AuthenticationProviders for exotic mechanisms: LDAP, OAuth2 tokens, hardware tokens, etc. The key is implementing authenticate() and supports() correctly.

sections.title: UserDetailsService
sections.content:
UserDetailsService is the interface Spring Security uses to load user-specific data during authentication. It has a single method: loadUserByUsername(String username), which returns a UserDetails object or throws UsernameNotFoundException. This is the bridge between Spring Security's authentication mechanism and your application's user storage (database, LDAP, in-memory, etc.).

The UserDetails interface represents the user information Spring Security needs: username, password (hashed), whether the account is enabled/expired/locked, and a collection of GrantedAuthority objects. Spring provides a built-in User class that implements UserDetails, or you can make your own entity class implement the interface directly.

GrantedAuthority objects represent roles and permissions. Roles conventionally have a ROLE_ prefix (ROLE_ADMIN, ROLE_USER), while authorities are finer-grained permissions (READ_PRODUCTS, DELETE_ORDERS). Both are stored as strings in GrantedAuthority. The distinction matters when using hasRole() vs hasAuthority() in your security rules — hasRole('ADMIN') automatically prepends ROLE_ and checks for ROLE_ADMIN, while hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN') checks the exact string.

In a real application your UserDetailsService implementation queries the database: find the user by username, map their roles from a roles table or roles column, build a list of SimpleGrantedAuthority objects, and construct the UserDetails. This is loaded once per authentication event — not on every request (for JWT apps the SecurityContext is rebuilt from the token, not from DB).

sections.title: PasswordEncoder
sections.content:
Never store plaintext passwords. This is one of the most fundamental security rules, and Spring Security enforces good practice through its PasswordEncoder interface. The interface has two key methods: encode(rawPassword) which returns a hashed string, and matches(rawPassword, encodedPassword) which verifies a submitted password against the stored hash — without ever decoding the hash.

BCryptPasswordEncoder is the recommended default. BCrypt is a deliberately slow hashing algorithm that automatically incorporates a random salt, making it resistant to rainbow table attacks. The cost factor (work factor) controls how slow it is — the default of 10 means 2^10 iterations. As CPUs get faster, you increase this factor to keep brute-force attacks expensive. The encoded string contains the salt and cost factor, so old passwords remain verifiable even after you increase the cost.

When a user registers, you call encoder.encode(rawPassword) before persisting. During login, DaoAuthenticationProvider calls encoder.matches(submittedPassword, storedHash). You never compare hashed strings directly with .equals() — hashes of the same password differ due to random salting.

DelegatingPasswordEncoder is Spring Security's latest recommendation: it prefixes the stored hash with the encoder identifier (e.g., {bcrypt}$2a$...), allowing you to migrate algorithms over time. PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() creates one that defaults to BCrypt but can verify passwords encoded with older algorithms (noop, sha256, etc.) for gradual migration.

sections.title: JWT Authentication Flow
sections.content:
JWT (JSON Web Token) authentication is the standard approach for stateless REST APIs. The flow has two phases: first the client authenticates and receives a JWT; then on every subsequent request the client sends that JWT and the server validates it — no session or database lookup needed per request.

In the login phase, the client sends credentials (username/password) to a login endpoint (e.g., POST /auth/login). Your controller delegates to AuthenticationManager.authenticate(), which validates via DaoAuthenticationProvider. On success, your code generates a JWT signed with a secret key, embeds the username and roles as claims, and returns the token to the client.

On subsequent requests, the client sends the JWT in the Authorization header as a Bearer token: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci.... A custom JwtAuthenticationFilter (extending OncePerRequestFilter) intercepts every request. It extracts the Bearer token, validates the signature and expiry, extracts the username and roles from claims, builds a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken with those authorities, and sets it in the SecurityContextHolder. Spring Security then sees an authenticated request and proceeds with authorization checks.

The crucial advantage is statelessness: the server holds no session state. Any server in a cluster can validate any token, making JWT ideal for microservices and horizontal scaling. The tradeoff is that tokens cannot be invalidated before expiry without additional infrastructure (a token blacklist or refresh token rotation with revocation).

sections.title: URL-based Authorization
sections.content:
URL-based authorization is configured in the SecurityFilterChain bean using the authorizeHttpRequests() DSL. You define a series of requestMatchers rules that map URL patterns to access requirements. Rules are evaluated in order — the first matching rule wins — so you should always put more specific rules before broader ones.

The four most common matchers are: permitAll() which allows any request (authenticated or not); authenticated() which requires any authenticated user; hasRole('ADMIN') which requires the ROLE_ADMIN authority; and hasAuthority('READ_REPORTS') which requires the exact authority string. The difference between roles and authorities is critical: hasRole('ADMIN') automatically prepends 'ROLE_' and looks for 'ROLE_ADMIN', while hasAuthority() checks the exact string you provide. So if you store 'ADMIN' without the prefix, use hasAuthority('ADMIN'), not hasRole('ADMIN').

Modern Spring Security (6.x) uses requestMatchers() instead of the deprecated antMatchers(). requestMatchers() is smarter about handling Spring MVC routing and avoids certain CVEs that antMatchers() was susceptible to with ambiguous path matching. The patterns support Ant-style wildcards: /api/** matches any path under /api/, /user/* matches exactly one path segment.

A common pattern for REST APIs: permit unauthenticated access to auth endpoints (/auth/login, /auth/register), permit public read endpoints, and require authentication for everything else. Always end your rules with .anyRequest().authenticated() or .anyRequest().denyAll() as a catch-all.

sections.title: Method-level Security
Expression-based Access Control
sections.content:
Spring Security integrates Spring Expression Language (SpEL) in @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize, enabling arbitrarily complex access control logic. The expressions are evaluated against a SecurityExpressionRoot that exposes security-specific variables and methods.

Built-in expressions include: hasRole('X') and hasAuthority('X') for role/authority checking; isAuthenticated() which returns true if the user is logged in; isAnonymous() for unauthenticated users; principal which gives the UserDetails object; authentication which gives the full Authentication object; permitAll and denyAll as constants.

You can reference method parameters by name using the # prefix: @PreAuthorize("#username == authentication.name") checks that the username parameter matches the logged-in user. This enables ownership checks without any database query. Parameter names are available if compiled with -parameters or if you use Spring's @P annotation.

For complex business rules, define a custom security service bean and call it from SpEL: @PreAuthorize("@documentSecurity.canRead(authentication, #docId)"). The @ symbol references a Spring bean. This approach keeps your annotation expressions readable and lets you write testable security logic in a regular Spring component. This pattern is recommended for any rule more complex than a simple role check.

sections.title: Custom Access Denied Handling
sections.content:
Spring Security throws two distinct exceptions when access fails, and they map to different HTTP status codes. AuthenticationException is thrown when the user is not authenticated (not logged in, invalid credentials, expired token) and should result in a 401 Unauthorized response. AccessDeniedException is thrown when the user IS authenticated but lacks the required permissions and should result in a 403 Forbidden response.

The ExceptionTranslationFilter sits in the filter chain and catches these exceptions. For AuthenticationException it delegates to an AuthenticationEntryPoint. The default entry point for form login redirects to /login; for REST APIs you want to return a JSON error body with 401. For AccessDeniedException it delegates to an AccessDeniedHandler.

Implementing custom handlers is straightforward. For AuthenticationEntryPoint, implement the commence() method: set the response status to 401, set Content-Type to application/json, and write a JSON error body. For AccessDeniedHandler, implement handle() similarly but with 403. Register both handlers in your HttpSecurity configuration via exceptionHandling().

A common mistake is returning 401 for access denied and 403 for unauthenticated — don't mix them up. HTTP 401 literally means "Unauthorized but unauthenticated" (the name is misleading), and 403 means "Forbidden — you are known but not allowed." Correct semantics matter for API clients.

sections.title: JWT Structure
sections.content:
A JSON Web Token is a compact, URL-safe string consisting of three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots: Header.Payload.Signature. Each part serves a distinct purpose in making the token self-contained and verifiable.

The Header is a JSON object describing the token type and signing algorithm: {"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}. Common algorithms are HS256 (HMAC with SHA-256, uses a symmetric secret key shared between issuer and verifier) and RS256 (RSA with SHA-256, uses an asymmetric key pair — private key signs, public key verifies). RS256 is preferred when different services need to verify tokens without holding the signing key.

The Payload contains claims — statements about the subject (user) and metadata. Registered claims have standardized names: sub (subject, usually the user ID or username), iat (issued at, a Unix timestamp), exp (expiration time, also a Unix timestamp), iss (issuer), aud (audience). Custom claims add your application-specific data: roles, userId, email. Keep the payload small — it is Base64URL encoded but NOT encrypted, so anyone can decode and read it. Never put passwords or sensitive data in a JWT payload.

The Signature is computed by the server: HMACSHA256(base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload), secret). When the server receives a token, it recomputes the signature and compares — if they match, the payload has not been tampered with. This is what makes JWTs trustworthy: modifying any claim invalidates the signature.

sections.title: JWT Validation
sections.content:
Validating a JWT involves three steps: verifying the signature, checking that the token has not expired, and extracting the claims for use in setting up the SecurityContext. Each step can fail independently, and each failure should be handled gracefully by returning a 401 response.

With the jjwt library (io.jsonwebtoken), validation is done via the Jwts.parser() builder. You provide the signing key; the parser automatically verifies the signature and throws SignatureException if it does not match, meaning the token was tampered with or signed with a different key. It also throws ExpiredJwtException if the exp claim is in the past.

After validation, you extract claims using .getPayload(). The Claims object is a Map with helper methods: getSubject() for the sub claim, getExpiration(), get("roles", List.class) for custom claims. The signing key must be at least 256 bits (32 bytes) for HS256 — store it as a Base64-encoded string in application.properties and decode it at startup; never hardcode it in source code.

For production systems, generate the secret key with a cryptographically secure random generator and manage it through environment variables or a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault). Rotating keys requires either immediate invalidation of all existing tokens or a grace period where you accept both old and new keys.

sections.title: Implementing JWT Filter
sections.content:
The JWT filter is the glue between your token validation logic and Spring Security's authentication model. It extends OncePerRequestFilter, a Spring utility that guarantees the filter runs exactly once per request even in complex servlet dispatch scenarios (unlike implementing Filter directly, which can run multiple times for forwards/includes).

The filter's doFilterInternal method follows a precise sequence: extract the Authorization header, check for the Bearer prefix, strip it to get the raw token, validate the token, extract user information, build an Authentication object, and set it in the SecurityContextHolder. If any step fails (no header, invalid token), the filter does not set authentication — it simply calls chain.doFilter() and continues. The authorization layer will then see an unauthenticated request and respond with 401.

A subtle but important detail: only set the SecurityContext if no authentication already exists — check SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() == null first. This prevents re-processing if another filter has already set the context. Another detail: the WebAuthenticationDetailsSource captures the client IP and session ID from the request, which is useful for auditing.

Register your filter in the SecurityFilterChain using http.addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class). This ensures JWT validation runs before Spring's form-login filter, so JWT-authenticated requests are handled correctly without attempting form-based login.

sections.title: Refresh Tokens
sections.content:
Short-lived access tokens (15 minutes to 1 hour) minimize the damage if a token is stolen — the attacker's window is limited. But forcing users to log in repeatedly is terrible UX. Refresh tokens solve this: a long-lived refresh token (days to weeks) is issued alongside the short-lived access token, and the client uses it silently to obtain new access tokens without re-entering credentials.

The refresh token should be stored server-side (database or Redis) linked to the user, allowing revocation. When a user logs out or changes their password, you delete their refresh tokens from storage, immediately invalidating all their sessions. This is something pure JWT cannot do without a blocklist. The refresh token itself can be an opaque random string (UUID) or a long-lived JWT, but opaque tokens with server-side storage are simpler to revoke.

The refresh flow: the client sends the refresh token to POST /auth/refresh. Your endpoint looks up the token in the database, checks it is not expired or revoked, finds the associated user, issues a new short-lived access token (and optionally a new refresh token — token rotation), and returns both. Refresh token rotation means each use of a refresh token issues a new one and invalidates the old, detecting token theft: if a stolen token is used after the legitimate user has rotated it, the now-invalid old token signals a compromise.

Store refresh tokens in httpOnly cookies for browser clients (prevents JavaScript XSS theft) or in secure storage for mobile apps. Never expose them to JavaScript. Access tokens can live in memory or localStorage, accepting the shorter exposure window.

sections.title: CSRF Protection
sections.content:
Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) is an attack where a malicious website tricks a user's browser into making authenticated requests to your server. Because browsers automatically send cookies with every request, if your app uses cookie-based sessions, a forged request from evil.com to bank.com will carry the user's session cookie, potentially performing actions on their behalf.

Spring Security's built-in CSRF protection uses the Synchronizer Token Pattern: the server generates a random CSRF token, stores it in the session, and includes it in all HTML forms as a hidden field (or in a cookie for Angular/React apps). The server validates this token on every state-changing request (POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH). Since evil.com cannot read the CSRF token from your domain (same-origin policy), the forged request will lack it and be rejected.

However, for stateless REST APIs that use JWT authentication (no cookies, no sessions), CSRF is not a threat. JWTs are stored in localStorage or in-memory, not cookies, so the browser will not automatically send them to forged requests. Enabling CSRF protection for a pure JWT REST API just adds complexity with no security benefit. The standard practice is to call csrf().disable() when using stateless JWT authentication.

If you have a hybrid app (server-rendered HTML forms AND a REST API), enable CSRF for the form-based endpoints and disable or exempt the API paths. Spring Security 6 changed csrf() to use the new lambda DSL: .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()) is the modern form.

sections.title: CORS Configuration
sections.content:
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a browser security feature that blocks web pages from making requests to a different domain than the one that served them. If your React frontend is at http://localhost:3000 and your Spring Boot API is at http://localhost:8080, every API call will be blocked by the browser unless the server explicitly permits cross-origin requests.

Before every non-simple cross-origin request, the browser sends a preflight OPTIONS request to ask if the actual request is allowed. Your server must respond with the appropriate Access-Control-Allow-* headers. Spring Security's CORS support handles this correctly — it must be configured BEFORE any authentication filters, because a failed preflight (no CORS headers) looks like an authentication failure.

The recommended approach is to define a CorsConfigurationSource bean and reference it in HttpSecurity. CorsConfiguration lets you set allowedOrigins (specific domains or * for all), allowedMethods (GET, POST, etc.), allowedHeaders, and whether credentials (cookies, Authorization header) are allowed via allowCredentials(true). Note: when allowCredentials is true, you cannot use allowedOrigins("*") — you must list specific origins.

In development you typically allow your frontend's local URL. In production, allow only your actual frontend domain. Never allow * with credentials in production — it would permit any site to make authenticated requests to your API.

sections.title: Session Management
sections.content:
Spring Security's session management controls whether and how HTTP sessions are used to store the SecurityContext between requests. The behavior is governed by SessionCreationPolicy, configured via sessionManagement() in HttpSecurity.

The four policies are: ALWAYS creates a session even if not needed; IF_REQUIRED (the default) creates a session when Spring Security needs to store authentication; NEVER means Spring Security will not create sessions but will use one if it already exists from elsewhere; STATELESS is the correct choice for JWT REST APIs — Spring Security will never create or use an HTTP session, storing nothing between requests.

For JWT APIs, STATELESS is essential for correctness and scalability. With STATELESS, there is no session-based memory or stickiness requirement on your load balancer. Every request is independent; authentication comes entirely from the JWT in the Authorization header. Without this setting, Spring Security might inadvertently create sessions and introduce confusing behavior.

For traditional session-based apps, you can configure concurrent session control (prevent more than N simultaneous sessions per user), session fixation protection (always create a new session ID after login to prevent session fixation attacks), and invalid session handling (redirect to a URL when the session expires). These features are irrelevant for stateless JWT apps but important for web application security.

sections.title: OAuth2 Resource Server
sections.content:
OAuth2 Resource Server support in Spring Security allows your application to act as a protected resource that validates Bearer tokens issued by an Authorization Server (e.g., Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, or a custom Spring Authorization Server). Unlike implementing your own JWT filter, the resource server support is declarative and handles all validation automatically.

With .oauth2ResourceServer().jwt(), Spring Security registers BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter which extracts the Bearer token from every request. It then uses a JwtDecoder to validate the token: verifying the signature, checking expiry, and parsing claims. The JwtDecoder is configured with the issuer URI (Spring fetches the JWKS — JSON Web Key Set — from the Authorization Server's well-known endpoint to get public keys) or with an explicit public key.

Claims from the JWT are automatically mapped to GrantedAuthority objects for use in authorization rules. The default mapping looks for a scope or scp claim (creating SCOPE_read, SCOPE_write authorities) and a roles claim. You can customize this with a JwtAuthenticationConverter that maps custom claim structures (e.g., Keycloak's realm_access.roles) to authorities.

This approach is recommended over hand-rolling a JWT filter when using a real OAuth2 Authorization Server, because it handles key rotation automatically (JWKS is refreshed periodically), implements the full OAuth2 bearer token spec, and requires much less boilerplate.
